title: Caesar Cipher
directAnswer: Shift each letter forward by k positions within its own case, wrapping past 'z'/'Z' back to the start, and leave every non-letter untouched. The wrap is modular arithmetic: newChar = base + (c − base + k) % 26, where base is 'a' for lowercase and 'A' for uppercase. Reduce k by k % 26 first so a huge k doesn't overflow. O(n) time, O(n) space for the output.

remember.pattern: Per-letter modular shift within its case
rules: Map a letter to its **0–25 offset** (`c − base`), add `k`, take `% 26`, then add `base` back — this is the wrap.
Use a **different base** per case: `'a'` for lowercase, `'A'` for uppercase. Mixing them garbles the case.
**Leave non-letters unchanged** — digits, spaces, and punctuation pass straight through.
Reduce `k %= 26` up front; a large `k` (e.g. 10⁹) is otherwise just wasted work and risks overflow in fixed-width arithmetic.
Preserve case: never uppercase or lowercase the whole string — shift each letter in its own alphabet.
whenToUse: A fixed rotation/shift over a cyclic alphabet (encrypt, ROT13, rotate digits)
Each element transforms independently based only on itself and a constant offset
Wrap-around behaviour ('past z goes to a') is required
Some elements must be skipped (non-letters) while others are mapped
antiSignals: The shift varies per position (e.g. Vigenère cipher) → use a key sequence, not one k
You must decrypt without knowing k → frequency analysis, not a fixed shift
Characters interact (e.g. transposition ciphers) → not an independent per-char map
Alphabet isn't 26 letters / isn't cyclic → the % 26 model breaks
remember.takeaway: Rotating over a fixed cyclic alphabet is textbook modular arithmetic: normalise to a 0-based offset, add the shift mod the alphabet size, re-base. Reducing the shift mod 26 first keeps it correct and cheap no matter how large k is.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you implement the wrap with modular arithmetic instead of brittle if-chains, keep the two cases separate, and skip non-letters cleanly.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Adding k to the character code without the modulo, so shifting 'y' by 5 produces a non-letter symbol instead of wrapping to 'd'.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Reduce k mod 26 first, derive the (c − base + k) % 26 + base formula explicitly, and mention the same idea generalises to ROT13 and digit rotation.

problemStatement: Given an unencrypted string `s` and a non-negative integer `k`, encrypt the string with a Caesar cipher: **shift each letter forward by `k` positions** in the alphabet, wrapping around from `z` back to `a` (and `Z` to `A`). Case must be preserved, and **non-letter characters are left unchanged**. Return the encrypted string.
constraints: 0 ≤ k ≤ 10⁹  (k can be far larger than 26)
s may contain letters, digits, spaces, and punctuation
Letter case must be preserved in the output
understanding: Each letter slides forward k slots inside its own 26-letter alphabet; falling off the end loops back to the beginning. Lowercase stays lowercase, uppercase stays uppercase, and anything that isn't a letter is copied verbatim. Because the alphabet is cyclic, shifting by k and by k mod 26 are identical — so reduce k first.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can k be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 10⁹. Since the alphabet is cyclic, k and k % 26 give the same result — reduce k first to avoid pointless work and overflow.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What happens to digits, spaces, and punctuation?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: They are left exactly as they are. Only alphabetic characters are shifted.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is case preserved?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. An uppercase letter shifts within A–Z and a lowercase letter within a–z; the case never flips.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are we encrypting (forward shift) or decrypting?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Encrypting — shift forward by k. To decrypt you'd shift by 26 − (k % 26), but the prompt asks for encryption.

27 % 26 = 1, so it's a shift of 1: a→b, b→c, c→d.

approaches.name: Manual Wrap with If-Chains (Naive)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to show the wrap logic explicitly, then replace it with one modulo to avoid the branch soup.
hints: Add k to the character code directly, then fix up overflow by hand: if it passes 'z', subtract 26.
You still have to reduce k first, or a single subtraction won't be enough when k > 26.
Notice how many edge branches you need (over 'z', over 'Z', wrap by more than once) — that's the smell the modulo removes.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Still one pass over n characters, O(n) time, and an O(n) output buffer. The cost is in correctness, not asymptotics — the branchy wrap is easy to get wrong.
approaches.explanation:
The hand-rolled version shifts a letter by adding `k` to its code and then patches the result back into range with explicit comparisons.

**Why people reach for it.** Without recalling modular arithmetic, the obvious move is: `c + k`, and if that lands past `'z'`, subtract `26` to wrap. It mirrors how you'd shift letters on paper.

**Where it goes wrong.** A single `if (x > 'z') x -= 26;` only undoes *one* wrap. If `k` (or `k % 26`) plus the offset overshoots the alphabet by more than 26 — which happens whenever you forget to reduce `k` first — one subtraction isn't enough, and you'd need a loop or repeated subtraction. You also have to duplicate the whole fix-up for uppercase. Every extra branch is a place for an off-by-one or a wrong base.

**Why we don't ship it.** It is the same `O(n)`, but it trades a clean one-line transform for a thicket of conditionals. The modular formula expresses the wrap exactly once and can never under- or over-shoot, so it is both shorter and safer. Show the if-chain to demonstrate you understand the wrap, then fold it into the modulo.
approaches.insight: If you ever write `if (x > 'z') x -= 26;`, you've re-implemented `% 26` by hand — and only the version that handles a single wrap. Reach for the modulo and reduce k first so a single operation always lands in range.

approaches.name: Modular Arithmetic Shift (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer. Say 'normalise to 0–25, add k, take mod 26, re-base' — one expression per case.
hints: Map each letter to a 0-based offset within its alphabet: lowercase offset = c − 'a'. What operation naturally wraps an offset back into 0–25?
(offset + k) % 26 wraps for free, no matter how far you shift. Then add the base back to return to a real character.
Reduce k %= 26 once at the start (k can be 10⁹), branch on case, leave non-letters alone.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass over the string, constant work per character (a couple of arithmetic ops and a branch), so O(n) time. The output buffer is O(n); the transformation itself uses O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
For each character, decide its class, then for letters apply one expression: `base + (c − base + k) % 26`, where `base` is `'a'` or `'A'`.

**Why subtract the base first.** Character codes for `'a'..'z'` are `97..122`, an awkward range to do arithmetic on. Subtracting `'a'` re-centres a lowercase letter onto `0..25`, the natural index inside the alphabet. Now `+ k` is a plain shift on those indices.

**Why `% 26` is the wrap.** After adding `k`, the index might be `≥ 26` (e.g. `'y'` is `24`, plus `2` is `26`). Taking `% 26` folds it back into `0..25` — `26 → 0` is exactly `'y' → 'a'`'s wrap. The modulo encodes 'past z loops to a' in one operation, and it works for *any* amount of overshoot, unlike a single subtraction.

**Why add the base back.** The result of `% 26` is an index in `0..25`; adding `base` returns it to a real character code in the correct case. Use `'A'` for uppercase so the case is preserved — never mix bases.

**Why reduce k mod 26 up front.** Shifting by `k` and by `k % 26` are identical on a 26-cycle, so collapsing `k` first keeps the numbers small (important in fixed-width languages where `c − base + 10⁹` could be a concern) and signals you understand the cyclic structure. After that, `(c − base + k) % 26` always lands in range with no special cases.

**Why non-letters fall through.** The branch only fires for `a–z` and `A–Z`; everything else is appended unchanged, satisfying 'leave non-letters alone' with no extra logic.
approaches.insight: The three-step idiom — normalise to a 0-based offset, do the arithmetic mod the cycle length, re-base — is the universal recipe for any rotation over a fixed alphabet. ROT13 is k = 13, rotating digits is the same with base '0' and % 10. Recognise the cycle and the modulo writes itself.

edgeCases.behavior: Shift of 0 returns the string unchanged.
'Z'→'A' and 'z'→'a' — both wrap within their own case.
No letters → output identical to input.

pitfalls: Omitting % 26 so 'y' + 5 becomes a punctuation code instead of 'd'.
Using a single base for both cases, flipping uppercase to lowercase.
Forgetting to reduce k, letting a 10⁹ shift bloat arithmetic or overflow fixed-width ints.

commonMistakes: Shifting without % 26, producing symbols past 'z'/'Z' instead of wrapping.
Lowercasing or uppercasing the whole string and losing the original case.
Accidentally shifting digits, spaces, or punctuation that should stay fixed.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the modulo (no wrap)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Adding k to the code without % 26 pushes letters near the end of the alphabet into non-letter codes — 'y' + 5 becomes '~' instead of 'd'.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Losing case by using one base
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Re-basing every letter to 'a' turns uppercase letters into lowercase, breaking the case-preservation rule.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: out.append(chr((ord(c) - ord('a') + k) % 26 + ord('a')))  # for ALL letters
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
base = ord('a') if c.islower() else ord('A')
out.append(chr((ord(c) - base + k) % 26 + base))

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Shifting non-letters
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you don't guard the branch, spaces and punctuation get shifted into other symbols, corrupting the output.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: out.append(chr((ord(c) - ord('a') + k) % 26 + ord('a')))  # even for ' ' and '-'

patternNote: Modular rotation over a fixed alphabet. Normalise each symbol to a 0-based index, add the shift, take it modulo the alphabet size to wrap, then re-base. Reduce the shift mod the cycle length first. The same recipe powers ROT13, digit rotation, and clock arithmetic.
